alt: A time axis from 1905 to 1947 with bars for each Key Question: KQ6 from 1905 to 1927, the Khilafat Movement (KQ7) from 1919 to 1924, KQ8 from 1927 to 1939 and KQ9 from 1940 to 1947. Markers show the League founded in 1906, the Lucknow Pact in 1916, the Nehru Report in 1928, the Lahore Resolution in 1940 and independence in 1947.
caption: Five Key Questions cover four overlapping periods and the three leaders who link them.

alt: Three stacked bars show the parts of a Section B question: a 4-mark knowledge part of one short paragraph, a 7-mark explanation part of at least two developed paragraphs, and a 14-mark evaluation essay of about two pages. Section A is a compulsory source-based question.
caption: Marks rise from recall to explanation to judgement, so answers must grow with them.

after: ## How did Muslim politics develop between 1905 and 1927? (Key Question 6)
alt: A vertical timeline from the 1905 Partition of Bengal through the Simla Deputation and founding of the Muslim League in 1906, the Morley–Minto Reforms of 1909, the reversal of partition in 1911, the Lucknow Pact of 1916, the events of 1919 and the divisions of the mid-1920s to the Delhi Proposals of 1927. Gains for the League are highlighted.
caption: Separate electorates were won early, but co-operation with Congress did not last.

after: ## Why did the Khilafat Movement fail? (Key Question 7)
alt: The aim of the Khilafat Movement, to protect the Ottoman caliph, sits above three events: failed delegations in 1920, the Hijrat to Afghanistan in 1920 and Gandhi’s Non-Cooperation link. Three reasons for failure follow: the Moplah uprising in 1921, Chauri Chaura in 1922 and the abolition of the caliphate in 1924. The impact was a loss of faith in Congress but a politically mobilised Muslim population.
caption: The movement failed in its aim but changed Muslim politics.

after: ## How successful was the Pakistan Movement between 1927 and 1939? (Key Question 8)
alt: A chain from the all-British Simon Commission of 1927 to the Nehru Report of 1928 and Jinnah’s 14 Points of 1929. A table compares them: the Nehru Report rejected separate electorates and one-third Muslim representation at the centre; the 14 Points kept both and asked for a federal constitution with provincial autonomy.
caption: The Nehru Report’s rejection of Muslim safeguards led directly to the 14 Points.

after: ## How successful was the Pakistan Movement between 1927 and 1939? (Key Question 8)
alt: A chain from the 1937 elections, where the League did poorly, to Congress rule from 1937 to 1939, which alienated Muslims through Bande Mataram, the Wardha and Vidya Mandir schemes and refusing to share power in the United Provinces. The ministries resigned in 1939, Jinnah called a Day of Deliverance on 22 December, and many Muslims became convinced they needed a separate homeland.
caption: A poor start in 1937 turned, through Congress rule, into support for a homeland.

after: ## How was independence achieved between 1940 and 1947? (Key Question 9)
alt: A vertical timeline from the Lahore Resolution of 23 March 1940 through the Cripps Mission and Quit India in 1942, the Gandhi–Jinnah talks of 1944, the Simla Conference of 1945, the 1945–46 elections, the Cabinet Mission and Direct Action Day in 1946 and the 3 June Plan to the Indian Independence Act of July 1947.
caption: Each failed solution after 1940 strengthened the case for partition.

after: ## How important were Jinnah, Iqbal and Rahmat Ali? (Key Question 10)
alt: Three columns. Jinnah moved from Hindu–Muslim unity to leading the League and turning the 1940 Resolution into a state. Iqbal gave Muslim nationhood its philosophical basis and proposed a North-Western Muslim state in 1930 but died in 1938. Rahmat Ali coined the name in 1933 and demanded complete separation but had little influence on League policy.
caption: Iqbal supplied the idea, Rahmat Ali the name, and Jinnah the leadership that made the state.
